# Mouse digit AAV gene delivery into fibroblasts regulates regenerative outcome

**Authors:** Vivian Jou; Scott D. Semelsberger; Jack Smerczynski; Jessica A. Lehoczky

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA. | 2Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA.

## Abstract

The distal mouse digit tip regenerates postamputation, while the proximal digit undergoes fibrosis. This study presents a comparative single-cell RNA sequencing–based analysis of regenerating and nonregenerating digits to computationally identify fibroblast subpopulations and genes associated with fibrosis and regeneration. To test the sufficiency of identified candidate genes to alter wound healing outcomes, we developed a robust adeno-associated virus gene delivery technique for digit fibroblasts. We found that overexpression of candidate profibrotic gene Pcolce2 or Prelp in the blastema modifies normal regeneration and overexpression of candidate proregenerative factor Ccl2 or Mest in the proximal digit substantially increases bone deposition. These data demonstrate that the computational analysis combined with the AAV delivery approach presented in this study provides a powerful framework for identifying the driving factors of fibrosis and regeneration in the mammalian digit.

## Abstract

AAV delivery of putative proregenerative genes into proximal, nonregenerative mouse digit fibroblasts induces regeneration.

## INTRODUCTION

The mouse digit tip is a robust model to study innate regeneration of composite tissues in mammals (1). Amputation through the distal phalangeal bone (P3; Fig. 1, A and C) results in the formation of a blastema followed by complete regeneration by 28 days postamputation (dpa) in adult mice (2, 3). Genetic lineage analyses and single-cell transcriptomic datasets have defined the cell type heterogeneity of the mouse digit tip blastema to broadly include immune, neural, vascular, and fibroblast cells (4–7). Fibroblasts, here defined as cells expressing Pdgfrα and Lumican, account for ~60% of the blastema and can be computationally categorized into at least 14 distinct subtypes (6). Previously, we identified 67 genes enriched in fibroblast subtypes that increased in population size in the blastema (6). Of these candidate proregenerative genes, we further investigated Mest and determined its expression to be specific to the blastema, not generic wound healing. With genetic loss of function experiments, we defined its role in the immune system to mediate proper bone regeneration (8). However, the sufficiency of Mest, and the other candidate genes, to induce regeneration remains unknown.

In contrast to the distal P3 digit tip, amputations through the proximal digit, such as through the proximal region of the P3 bone or mid-digitally through the second phalangeal bone (P2; Fig. 1, A to C), do not regenerate and instead heal via fibrosis (9–13). Because the P2 and P3 digits segments are physically distinct, the P2 digit amputation model is ideally suited for comparing regenerative and fibrotic fibroblasts and for regenerative sufficiency experiments (13, 14). To this point, previous studies have noted innate differences between P2 and P3 fibroblasts, although these studies did not address fibroblast heterogeneity or subtype-specific gene expression and function (7, 15). A comprehensive comparative analysis of fibroblast subtypes, their gene expression, putative functions, and population dynamics in P3 regeneration versus P2 fibrosis remains to be done. Separately, the P2 digit amputation is also an ideally suited platform to functionally test the sufficiency of candidate genes to induce regeneration in innately nonregenerative tissues. Previous studies have introduced exogenous factors including induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), proteins, and extracellular matrix (ECM) components into P2 postamputation wounds using techniques including conditional genetics, bead implantation, direct injection, or systemic delivery (16–20). While these reports collectively suggest that full regeneration can be induced from a P2 amputation given the correct combination of exogenous factors, the now used techniques lack the flexibility and scalability needed for higher-throughput screening of candidate genes.

Here, we present single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) time courses for stage-matched mouse P2 and P3 postamputation digits and directly compare fibroblast subtypes throughout digit fibrosis and digit tip regeneration. We find that P2 and P3 postamputation digits are enriched for distinct fibroblast subtypes, indicating innate cell type differences between digit fibrosis and regeneration. Hypothesizing that genes differentially expressed between P2 and P3 subtypes play a role in determining the P2 fibrosis or P3 regeneration phenotypes, we identified 98 candidate profibrotic and 27 candidate proregenerative genes. Toward unbiased, higher throughput functional assessment of these candidate genes induce P2 fibrosis– or P3 regeneration–associated phenotypes, we developed fibroblast-specific adeno-associated virus (AAV)–mediated gene delivery for local, transient gene expression. As proof of concept, we evaluated the sufficiency of three candidate profibrotic genes to inhibit regeneration following P3 amputations and of three candidate proregenerative genes to induce regeneration following P2 amputations. We demonstrate that AAV delivery of candidate profibrotic ECM regulator gene Pcolce2 or Prelp into blastemal fibroblasts alters three-dimensional (3D) bone morphology during regeneration and that AAV delivery of blastemal gene Ccl2 or Mest into P2 fibroblasts induces bone regeneration in the nonregenerative digits.

## RESULTS

### Distinct fibroblast subtype heterogeneity in P2 fibrosis versus P3 regeneration yields candidate genes for functional testing

To assess fibroblast heterogeneity during fibrosis of the P2 postamputation digit, we performed scRNA-seq of unamputated (UA) and 12, 17, and 28 dpa P2 wild-type FVB/NJ mouse digits. The genetic background and time points were matched to our previously reported P3 digit tip blastema dataset (GSE143888) to facilitate direct comparison of fibroblast subtypes (6). Following sequencing, quality control, and filtering, 11834 (UA), 7208 (12 dpa), 8268 (17 dpa), and 11752 (28 dpa) P2 cells were used for analysis (fig. S1, A to D). Canonical markers were used to assign broad cluster identities (fig. S1E), revealing cell type heterogeneity at all time points, consisting of fibroblast, immune, vascular smooth muscle, endothelial, and epithelial cells (fig. S1, A to D). Epithelial cells were underrepresented because of minimized epidermis collection during digit dissection. Integration of UA, 12, 17, and 28 dpa scRNA-seq data reinforced the cell type heterogeneity found in the homeostatic and fibrosing P2 digit (Fig. 1D), and while distinct in genetic background, stage, and cell type proportions, our results were consistent with GSE135985 (fig. S1F) (7).

To specifically address fibroblast heterogeneity, we subsetted and reclustered all P2 fibroblasts, which resulted in 19 computationally defined clusters, indicative of subpopulations as was found in the P3 digit blastema (Fig. 1E). Consistent with the P2 digit undergoing fibrosis, the total proportion of fibroblasts significantly increased at all postamputation stages as compared to the UA digit (Fig. 1F). To identify which fibroblast subtypes predominate at various stages, we assessed their population proportions over time. Differential proportion analysis (21), a statistical test developed to detect significant changes in scRNA-seq population sizes while accounting for experimental noise, revealed that clusters 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10, and 12 were the only clusters that exhibited significant population changes during fibrosis (Fig. 1, E and G). While each cluster had a distinct population dynamic profile, they broadly fell into three categories. (i) The fibroblast clusters 0, 4, 5, and 8 decreased in proportion at 12 dpa and then increased by 17 dpa or 28 dpa. Analysis of cluster-specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and Gene Ontology (GO) terms suggests that clusters 0, 4, 5, and 8 are associated with ECM organization, myeloid cell differentiation, ossification, and metabolism regulation, respectively (Fig. 1, G and H, and table S1). (ii) The fibroblast clusters 1, 3, and 10 increased in proportion at 12 dpa and then became depleted at 17 dpa and 28 dpa; these populations are predicted to be involved in collagen organization, guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase) activity, and mitosis, respectively (Fig. 1, G and H, and table S1). (iii) Cluster 12, which is associated with tissue development, was the only population to be depleted at all postamputation time points (Fig. 1G, fig. S1G, and table S1). We verified that the top DEGs associated with each significant cluster were also differentially expressed across time; for example, Fbn2 is a significant DEG at 12 dpa for cells in clusters 1 and 3, while Pcolce2 is a significant DEG at 28 dpa for cells in clusters 0 and 4 (fig. S1, H and I, and table S2). Appropriately, Fbn2 is significantly down-regulated at 28 dpa, while Pcolce2 is down-regulated in the UA and 12 dpa digits (table S2). These results suggest that, similar to digit tip regeneration, different fibroblast subpopulations with distinct biological functions contribute to varying stages of wound healing.

To determine how fibroblast subtypes correlate between P2 fibrosis and P3 regeneration, we integrated our stage matched P2 and P3 scRNA-seq datasets (UA, 12, 17, and 28 dpa; fig. S2, A to D). Common cell type heterogeneity was found between the P2 and P3 tissues; however, the proportions of these populations varied significantly (fig. S2, A’ to D’). Notably, total P3 fibroblasts were 3.1×, 2.1×, 1.5×, and 2× more populous as compared to all P2 fibroblasts at homeostasis, 12 dpa, 17 dpa, and 28 dpa, respectively (fig. S2, A’ to D’). Fibroblasts at each matched time point from the P2-P3 integrated dataset were subsetted and reclustered for comparative analysis of subpopulations (Fig. 2, A to D). While P2- and P3-derived cells were found in all clusters, the mixing was notably nonhomogeneous (Fig. 2, A’ to D’). As with all scRNA-seq experiments, despite the P2 and P3 samples being treated identically, modest cell dissociation and capture bias may exist. However, differential proportion analysis revealed that there were 10 UA, 3 12 dpa, 7 17 dpa, and 10 28 dpa fibroblast subpopulations significantly skewed in proportion between P2 and P3 tissues (Fig. 2, E to H). This suggests that P2 and P3 fibroblasts are quite distinct, even in homeostasis, corroborating previous studies (7, 15). To further support this computational finding in vivo, we performed RNA hybridization chain reaction fluorescent in situ hybridization (HCR-FISH) on P2 and P3 digit sections for DEGs Pi16 and Anxa8 (fig. S3). By scRNA-seq, Pi16 is expressed in UA P2 fibroblast clusters 2 and 7 and not in any other cell types (fig. S3, A and B). Accordingly, by HCR-FISH, Pi16 is not expressed in UA P3 digit tip (fig. S3C) but is expressed in the P2 dermis surrounding the dorsal hair follicles and ventral sweat glands and P3 toe pad (fig. S3, C to F). By scRNA-seq, Pi16 remains absent in the 28 dpa P3 tip (fig. S3G), and Anxa8 is expressed in 28 dpa P2 epithelium and fibroblasts with enrichment in fibroblast clusters 2 to 4, 12, and 13 (fig. S3, H and I). HCR-FISH on 28 dpa digits finds no Pi16 expression in the regenerated P3 (fig. S3J). In 28 dpa P2 amputated digits, both Anxa8 and Pi16 are expressed in the dermis (fig. S3K) with fibroblasts expressing neither gene, both genes (fig. S3K’, white arrow), primarily Anxa8 (fig. S3K, white arrow with green outline), or primarily Pi16 (fig. S3K, white arrow with pink outline). This heterogeneity revealed spatial restriction whereby Anxa8-enriched fibroblasts were directly adjacent to the distal edge of the 28 dpa P2 bone, while Pi16-expressing fibroblasts were enriched in the more distal dermis (fig. S3, K to K”).

To assign putative function to these P2- or P3-enriched subpopulations, we performed GO term and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment (Fig. 2, I to K, and fig. S2, E to G). Broadly over all postamputation stages, there were P3-enriched fibroblast subtypes with gene signatures of bone development and ossification, while there were P2-enriched fibroblast subtypes involved in GTPase-mediated signaling and cell adhesion (Fig. 2, I to K). In addition, up-regulated pathways in immune response, such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-17 signaling, were associated with 12 dpa and 17 dpa P3-enriched fibroblast subtypes, but at 28 dpa, this biological profile is associated with the P2 fibroblast subtype in cluster 5 (fig. S2, E to G). This suggests prolonged inflammation in the P2 wound, a canonical characteristic of the fibrotic response in many organs (22, 23). Separately, ECM organization GO terms were found for both P2 and P3 fibroblast subpopulations at 17 dpa and 28 dpa. The genes significantly associated with this GO term differed between P2 and P3 fibroblasts, suggesting distinct ECM environments between regeneration and fibrosis (fig. S2H).

For downstream in vivo analysis, we sought to define candidate profibrotic genes associated with P2-enriched fibroblast subtypes and candidate proregenerative genes associated with P3-enriched fibroblast subtypes. All P2 and P3 fibroblasts, including those from our previously reported 11 dpa and 14 dpa P3 blastema dataset were computationally integrated and clustered (fig. S2, I and J) (6). To identify candidate profibrotic genes, we isolated the DEGs from 28 dpa significantly enriched P2 clusters (28 dpa clusters 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, and 12; Fig. 2H and table S3) with a minimum percentage of cells greater than 0.25, an average log2 fold change greater than 0.58, and an adjusted P value less than 0.05. As fibrosis is a chronic process, we chose the latest matched time point of 28 dpa to identify candidate profibrotic genes. These genes were filtered for those highly up-regulated in 28 dpa P2 fibroblasts as compared to UA, 12 dpa, and 17 dpa P2 fibroblasts (table S2). Of the resulting 98 candidate profibrotic genes (table S4), we selected Ccn3 (cellular communication network factor 3), Pcolce2 (procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer 2), and Prelp (prolargin; proline/arginine rich end leucine rich repeat protein) for further assessment (Fig. 2, L and M). Separately, to identify candidate proregenerative genes, we isolated the DEGs from 12 dpa significantly enriched P3 clusters (12 dpa clusters 1 and 2; Fig. 2F and table S5) with a minimum percentage of cells greater than 0.25, an average log2 fold change greater than 0.58, and an adjusted P value less than 0.05. These genes were further filtered on the basis of our previously identified blastema-enriched genes and resulted in 27 candidate proregenerative genes (table S6). Ccl2 (C-C motif chemokine ligand 2), Cxcl2 (C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 2), and Mest (mesoderm specific transcript) were selected for functional testing (6). Ultimately, these two lists of genes represent factors that may be integral in determining whether the tissue heals via fibrosis or regeneration.

### AAV2/6 injection yields robust transient gene expression in digit fibroblasts

Our comparative analysis of P2 and P3 fibroblast subtypes identified numerous putative profibrotic and proregenerative candidate genes (tables S4 and S6). Ideally, every candidate gene would be evaluated in vivo; however, existing techniques for gene or protein modulation in mouse digits are limited by reagents and throughput. In turn, we sought to develop a flexible, higher-throughput, gene candidate screening platform for the digit and turned to AAVs. In recent years, AAVs have become a popular tool for gene delivery due to their nonpathogenicity, flexibility in cell type tropism, and scalability for large studies (24–27). We began by assessing five pseudotypes of AAV-CAG-GFP: 6, 8, 9, 7m8, and PHP.S, chosen based on previous studies supporting infectivity in mesenchymal cells (27–30). Five cohorts of wild-type adult mice underwent distal digit tip amputations (P3 regeneration; Fig. 1A), while separate cohorts underwent mid-digital amputations (P2 fibrosis; Fig. 1A). At 6 dpa, when the epithelium has covered the wound, 2 μl of high titer AAV (>1 × 1013 vg/ml) was injected locally via Hamilton syringe, using one serotype per P2 or P3 cohort (fig. S4A). All digits were analyzed for green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression at 12 dpa [6 days postinjection (dpi)], and results were consistent between P2 and P3 tissues. While minimal GFP expression was found following AAV8 or AAV9 infections, significant expression was found in the AAV6-, 7m8-, and PHP.S-injected digits (Fig. 3, A to D). AAV6 infection resulted in 11.2× and 4.0× increases in GFP expression than AAV8 in the P2 and P3 digits, respectively, and 271.6× and 4.8× increases versus AAV9 in the P2 and P3 digits, respectively (Fig. 3, A to D). Colabeling of GFP and Vimentin (VIM) expression indicates that both AAV6 and AAV7m8 infect primarily mesenchymal with more than 80% of GFP-positive cells also expressing VIM (fig. S4, B to D). In addition, AAV6 infection is concentrated around the digit injection site (fig. S4, E to H) and infects RUNX2+ cells, with an average of 55% GFP-positive cells also coexpressing RUNX2 in the P3-regenerating digit (fig. S4, I to I”). No GFP expression colocalizes with the epidermis or F4/80+ macrophages (fig. S4, J to K’) in either the P2 or P3 amputation model. To move forward with our experiments, we selected AAV6 for its high infectivity of mesenchymal cells in both P3 and P2 postamputation digits, although other pseudotypes such as AAV7m8 could be used for repeat AAV infection strategies to avoid potential antibody response to AAV6.

To determine the postinjection timing of AAV6-CAG-GFP expression, we assessed GFP expression at additional time points of 1, 3, 8, 10, 14, and 18 dpi (7, 9, 14, 16, 20, and 24 dpa, respectively) (Fig. 3, E and F, and fig. S4, L and M). For both P2 and P3 postamputation digits, several cells adjacent to the injection site express GFP as early as 1 dpi (Fig. 3, E and F). In P3-regenerating digits, there is an 8.7× increase in GFP/4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) signal at 3 dpi (Fig. 3E and fig. S4L; 1 versus 3 dpi, P = 2.1 × 10−7), and this expression persists until 10 dpi, when GFP expression decreases by 3.6× from 8 dpi (Fig. 3E and fig. S4L; 8 versus 10 dpi, P = 7.1 × 10−5). In P2 fibrosing digits, there is a 5.5× increase from 1 dpi to 3 dpi (1 versus 3 dpi, P = 4.7 × 10−6), and peak GFP signal is found at 6 dpi (Fig. 3F and fig. S4M). Expression then significantly decreases at each subsequent time point, with the most significant drop in GFP signal occurring between 8 and 10 dpi (1.9× decrease, P = 9.8 × 10−4). By 14 dpi, GFP expression is restricted to only a few sparse cells (Fig. 3F and fig. S4M). Thus, in both P2 and P3 digits, the maximum overexpression window is from 3 to 10 dpi.

To assure no AAV-related phenotypes were found, we compared infected and untreated P2 and P3 digits. To assess P3 bone regeneration, untreated and AAV-GFP–infected P3 digit tips were analyzed at 28 dpa (22 dpi) by quantification of alizarin red skeletal staining (Fig. 3, G and H). No significant differences were found in area or length of the P3 bone, indicating that AAV infection itself does not perturb regeneration (Fig. 3, I and J). To determine whether there was any AAV infection–related change in bone repair between untreated and AAV-GFP–infected P2 digits, we analyzed differential calcein and alizarin complexone staining (Fig. 3, K and L). Unlike the P3 digit tip, the absence of reliable P2 anatomical landmarks results in subtle amputation position variation, thus these vital bone dyes can clearly delineate preamputation (green) and postamputation (red) bone. Quantification of area and length of new bone growth revealed no significant differences between untreated and AAV-GFP–infected 28 dpa P2 digits (Fig. 3, M and N). These results demonstrate that AAV6 is a robust and efficient tool to use for local and transient gene expression manipulation in both P2 and P3 postamputation digit fibroblasts.

### AAV delivery of P2-derived candidate profibrotic genes to P3 blastema alters regeneration

To determine whether gene expression specific to P2-enriched fibroblast subtypes functions in driving fibrosis and/or repressing regeneration, we aimed to leverage this AAV delivery platform to screen our computationally identified candidates (tables S4 and S6). As proof of principle, we tested three of our computationally identified candidate profibrotic genes: Ccn3, Pcolce2, and Prelp (table S4). As described above, these were chosen for their distinct expression in fibroblasts in P2 tissue (fig. S5, A to C) with significant enrichment in fibrotic subclusters (Fig. 2, L and M). In addition, all three genes encode matrisome-associated proteins with distinct functions in fibrosis: CCN3 is a glycoprotein that has been shown to both promote and inhibit fibrosis in various tissue models, PCOLCE2 is a procollagen processing enzyme found to promote cardiac fibrosis, and PRELP is a member of the small leucine-rich proteoglycan family and found enriched in heart, liver, and adipose tissue fibrosis (31–40). High titer AAV6 was produced for mouse Ccn3, Pcolce2, and Prelp cDNA constructs (>1 × 1013 vg/ml). Mice underwent distal P3 amputations, and at 6 dpa, each experimental digit was injected with 2 μl of a single recombinant AAV. Eighteen infected digits from each cohort were collected at 6 dpi to validate AAV-derived expression by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis. Compared to AAV-GFP–infected control digits, we observed 9624×, 157×, and 171× increases in Ccn3, Pcolce2, and Prelp expression, respectively (fig. S5, D to F).

The digits from remaining mice of all cohorts were analyzed at 28 dpa (22 dpi) for any regenerative phenotypes. Masson’s trichrome histology reveals that all digits in each treatment group regenerated with no gross tissue composition differences (fig. S5, G to J). Additional digits were assessed by alizarin red skeletal staining for P3 2D bone area and length quantification (Fig. 4, A to D). AAV-Ccn3–infected digits exhibited no significant change in either bone area or length as compared to AAV-GFP digits (Fig. 4, B, E, and F). In contrast, 28 dpa AAV-Prelp–infected digits were 7% shorter in bone length as compared to AAV-GFP–infected digits (Fig. 4, D to F; P = 0.036), consistent with inhibiting regeneration. Unexpectedly, 28 dpa AAV-Pcolce2–infected digits had 11% increased bone area and 10% increased bone length as compared to AAV-GFP–infected digits (Fig. 4, C and E, F; P = 9.10 × 10−5 and 2.90 × 10−4, respectively).

To further determine any phenotypic changes in the 3D structure of these digits, we performed micro-computed tomography (microCT) analysis on these bones (Fig. 4, G to J). No significant differences were found in volume or surface area of the 28 dpa P3 bones for any of AAV-Ccn3, Pcolce2, or Prelp cohorts as compared to the AAV-GFP digits (fig. S5, K and L). These data were counterintuitive given the 2D bone area and length findings for AAV-Pcolce2– and AAV-Prelp–infected digits (Fig. 3, E and F). Thus, we reasoned that differences along the anterior-posterior (A-P) axis could account for unchanged volumes and surface areas. While the dorsal-ventral (D-V) measurements were consistent across treatment groups [Fig. 4, G to K; multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), P = 0.0534], the A-P bone widths significantly differed with the overexpressed gene (Fig. 4, G’ to J’ and L; MANOVA, P = 0.012). Notably, as compared to AAV-GFP–infected digits, AAV-Pcolce2 bones were significantly thinner, while AAV-Prelp bones were thicker throughout the proximal-distal (P-D) bone length (Fig. 4L). These A-P data reconcile the 2D bone length and 3D bone volume and surface area findings. Thus, while none of these candidate profibrotic genes were individually sufficient to fully inhibit regeneration, Prelp and Pcolce2 overexpression affected the 3D structure of the regenerated bone, supporting a role in collagen remodeling and bone deposition.

### P2 bone regeneration is induced by AAV delivery of candidate proregenerative genes

To identify whether genes specific to the enriched P3 blastemal fibroblast subtypes function to stimulate regeneration and/or suppress fibrosis, we used AAV infection in nonregenerating P2 amputations. As proof of principle, we tested three genes from our computationally identified proregenerative candidates (Fig. 2, N and O, and table S6): Ccl2, Cxcl2, and Mest. These genes were selected for their high enrichment in blastemal fibroblast clusters (tables S5 and S6 and fig. S6, A to C) as described above. Furthermore, CCL2 specifically recruits macrophages and was found to promote regeneration in tissues such as the heart, articular cartilage, and bone; CXCL2 recruits neutrophils and stimulates liver regeneration; MEST is necessary for proper immune cell recruitment and clearance to support digit tip regeneration (8, 41–45). Mouse Ccl2, Cxcl2, and Mest cDNAs were cloned and used to produce high titer AAV6 for injection (>1 × 1013 vg/ml). Four cohorts of adult wild-type mice underwent P2 digit amputations. At 6 dpa, 2 μl of AAV was injected into the healing digit, one gene per mouse/cohort. Eighteen digits from each cohort were collected at 6 dpi (12 dpa) to verify AAV-derived gene expression with qPCR and revealed a 23.4×, 5.7×, and 3.4× increase of Ccl2, Cxcl2, and Mest expression as compared to AAV-GFP–infected digits, respectively (fig. S6, D to F).

To characterize the sufficiency of each gene to promote regeneration, 28 dpa (22 dpi) P2 bones were analyzed following AAV-Ccl2, AAV-Cxcl2, or AAV-Mest infection. Masson’s trichrome staining revealed that AAV-Mest–infected digits had an aggregation of connective tissue abutting the distal repaired bone, which was significantly larger and unlike the distal tissue found in any of the other cohorts (Fig. 5, A to E). While Safranin O/Fast Green staining indicated that these cells were not chondrocytes (fig. S6G), some of these cells expressed the osteoblast marker SP7, beyond what was found in the AAV-GFP–infected digits (fig. S6, H and I). This indicates an enrichment of osteolineage cells in the AAV-Mest digits; thus, we aimed to quantify the amount of bone repair using differential calcein and alizarin complexone fluorescence (Fig. 5, F to I, and fig. S6, J to J”’). AAV-Ccl2–infected digits averaged a 36% increased area and 12% increased length for new bone as compared to the AAV-GFP–injected digits; however, these findings were not statistically significant perhaps due to the interdigit variation (Fig. 5, G, J, and K). Consistent with our hypothesis and prior reports supporting Mest as a proregenerative gene (6, 8), AAV-Mest–infected digits exhibited a 65% increased area and 25% increased length of P2 bones compared to AAV-GFP controls (Fig. 5, I to K; P = 4.8 × 10−4 and 2.5 × 10−3, respectively). This suggests that while up-regulated in blastemal fibroblasts, overexpression of Cxcl2 alone does not promote regeneration, although additional research is required to determine its exact role in digit wound healing.

## DISCUSSION

In this study, we aimed to identify fibroblast subpopulations and associated genes specific to P2 digit fibrosis or P3 digit regeneration. Toward this goal, we have generated two valuable resources for the field: (i) a strain and stage matched scRNA-seq–derived dataset through digit fibrosis and regeneration and (ii) a highly effective AAV-based local gene delivery technique to manipulate postamputation digit gene expression in vivo. As a proof of concept, we focused on fibroblasts and related genes; however, the dataset and techniques used here are broadly applicable to the community to assess differences in fibrosis and regeneration in all cell types in the mouse digit. Our P2 digit scRNA-seq analysis yielded more than 12,000 fibroblasts from UA, 12, 17, and 28 dpa samples (Fig. 1E). Consistent with our characterization of P3 digit tip fibroblasts (6), we also find fibroblast subtype heterogeneity among P2-derived fibroblasts with different population dynamics throughout fibrosis (Fig. 1, E and G). We hypothesized that there are fibroblast subtypes that are enriched in P3 regeneration and/or P2 fibrosis and underlie these responses. Following computational integration, we identified P2- and P3-enriched subpopulations at each matched time point (Fig. 2). While the skewing of some fibroblast subtypes could be attributed to anatomical differences between the P2 and P3 digits, we experimentally limited this possibility by minimizing dissection of P3 epidermis (nail organ and sweat glands) and P2 tendons. Instead, the proportion of fibroblast subtypes residing the homeostatic P2 versus P3 digit may serve as a signature of regenerative potential (Fig. 2, A’ and E). To explore this further, we focused on the fibroblast subtypes that were significantly skewed toward P2 fibrosis in a population size at 12 dpa, 17 dpa, or 28 dpa to identify candidate profibrotic and proregenerative genes. Ultimately, we identified 98 putative profibrotic genes and 27 putative proregenerative genes (tables S4 and S6). Most candidate proregenerative genes, which included many of our previously reported blastemal-enriched genes (6), are involved in the immune response. Furthermore, we found that up-regulation of inflammation-related pathways initially enriched in the blastema in 28 dpa P2 fibroblasts, suggesting a later-stage inflammatory response in fibrosis (fig. S2, E to G). This finding corroborates previous studies establishing chronic inflammation as a hallmark of fibrosis in other models (22, 23) and may prove important in developing new therapies for fibrosis. However, future research to determine the genes initiating fibrosis versus regeneration by analysis of P2 and P3 DEGs at earlier time points, such as 12 dpa or prior, will be important to the field.

To evaluate the biological role our computationally identified candidate genes may have, we developed and validated the usage of recombinant AAV6-based gene delivery to the postamputation mouse P2 and P3 digits. We demonstrate that this method is ideal for local, transient gene expression in fibroblasts, with the highest expression from 3 to 10 days postinfection (Fig. 3). While we only used AAV6 for single injections, utilization of different AAV pseudotypes for co- or repeat injection strategies, such as AAV7m8 (Fig. 3 and fig. S4D), is possible. Furthermore, our studies were focused on infecting fibroblasts, but this injection technique using different AAV pseudotypes will facilitate gene manipulation in other cell types. In addition, timing of injection can be adjusted for desired gene overexpression temporal profile. This tool is a major step forward for unbiased functional assessment of candidate genes or other genetic manipulation such as knockdown, CRISPR-based perturbations, reporter systems, or inducible constructs in the digit fibroblasts.

In testing our computationally identified profibrotic genes, 28 dpa AAV-Pcolce2–infected digits had longer and larger bones along the P-D axis but thinner along the A-P axis. AAV-Prelp had the reverse effect, with shorter bones that were slightly wider (Fig. 4). While both are matrisome-associated genes (31), how they modulate bone shape is unknown. PRELP is expressed in myofibroblasts to increase collagen production to promote fibrosis and was shown to stiffen the ECM in zebrafish central nervous system wound healing, which may explain the shorter bones due to physical constraints (39, 46, 47). PCOLCE2 is an enzyme in procollagen cleaving also shown to have increased expression in myocardial fibrosis, although how it affected the digit bone 3D structure remains unknown (37, 38). In assessing our computationally identified proregenerative genes, Ccl2 and Mest overexpression resulted in increased P2 bone growth at 28 dpa (Fig. 5). These results complement our previous finding in which genetic knockout of Mest resulted in delayed bone regeneration (8). CCL2 attracts macrophages and monocytes (41) and has been shown to promote regeneration in other models (42–44). Whether CCL2 and MEST are acting in the same pathway to promote bone growth is unknown. In contrast, AAV-Cxcl2–injected digits had very little bone growth, resulting in stunted bones (Fig. 5). This inhibitory effect on digit bone repair may be due to the role of CXCL2 as a potent chemoattractant for neutrophils (41), for which increased and prolonged population has been associated with impaired wound healing (48). However, the changes in immune cell populations with overexpression of these given genes are still unclear and would require future studies to understand their roles in digit bone repair. In addition, to further enhance regeneration, it would be necessary to test additional genes or treat with combination of genes.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Experimental design

This study uses cohorts of adult wild-type FVB/NJ mice to generate P2 and P3 digit amputations for use in tissue generation for scRNA-seq experiments and separately for AAV gene delivery and subsequent analyses. All mice used in this study were housed in the Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) Hale Building for Transformative Medicine (BTM) vivarium maintained by the Center for Comparative Medicine. All mouse protocols and procedures were approved by the BWH Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee for protocol 2016 N000382. Eight- to 10-week-old male and female FVB/NJ mice (JAX, #001800) were used for all experiments in this study.

### Digit tip surgeries and AAV injections

For digit amputation surgeries, mice were anesthetized using inhaled 1 to 2% isoflurane in oxygen. Under stereomicroscope visualization, hindlimb digits 2, 3, and 4 were amputated using a sterile #11 scalpel. P3 digit tip regenerative amputations removed half of the third phalangeal segment; P2 nonregenerative digit amputations were made midway through the second phalangeal segment. Subcutaneous meloxicam (5 mg/kg) and buprenorphine HCl (0.05 mg/kg) were given for pre- and postsurgical analgesia.

For AAV injections, mice were anesthetized using inhaled 1 to 2% isoflurane and given meloxicam (5 mg/kg) for analgesia. For all AAV serotypes and constructs, 2 μl of high titer (>1 × 1013 vg/ml) AAV was directly injected into each digit at 6 dpa using a 5-ul Hamilton syringe and 33-gauge removable 0.5-inch (1.27 cm) needle with a 12-degree bevel. To validate pseudotype infection specificity and amount, three digits on the right hindpaw were injected with the same AAV-GFP pseudotype, while the left hindpaw digits remained untouched. For all other studies, all six digits on each mouse were injected with the same pseudotype and recombinant AAV. Mice who received the same AAV were cohoused.

### Single-cell RNA sequencing

For each scRNA-seq time point (UA, 12 dpa, 17 dpa, and 28 dpa), stage-specific P2 digit tissue was dissected and pooled from four mice (24 digits). Dissections were performed under microscopy to minimize epidermis and tendons; UA homeostatic tissue was collected from the tissue along the P2 bone. Single-cell suspensions for each time point were generated as previously described (6), with the addition of propidium iodide for live-cell sorting. In short, each pooled sample underwent enzymatic digestion with 2.5% trypsin and 10% collagenase followed by trituration by pipet. Red blood cells were removed with ammonium-chloride-potassium (ACK) lysing buffer, and cell suspension was strained twice through a 35-μm filter. Each sample was suspended in 0.4% bovine serum albumin/phosphate-buffered saline with propidium iodide (1 μg/μl). The BD FACS Aria sorter was used to collect propidium iodide–negative cells for each time point. Single-cell droplet encapsulation and library construction were performed at the BWH Center for Cellular Profiling using the 10X Chromium single-cell gene expression platform (10x Genomics). Single-cell 3′ v3 chemistry (10x Genomics) chemistry was used to generate cDNA libraries, and all libraries were sequenced by Illumina NextSeq 500 at the Dana Farber Cancer Institute Molecular Biology Core Facility.

### scRNA-seq computational analyses

Computational analyses were performed using the O2 high-performance computing environment maintained by the Research Computing Group at Harvard Medical School. For each P2 dataset, CellRanger 7.1.0 (10x Genomics) was used to align raw FASTQ files to the mouse mm10-2020-A reference transcriptome, with introns. Subsequent analyses were performed with Seurat v5.1.0 (49) package for R v4.3.1 (50). Raw data for UA, 12, 17, and 28 dpa samples contained 16,045, 8813, 10,514, and 15,253 sequenced cells that contained 67,080, 32,630, 23,539, and 15,585 mean reads per cell, respectively. Low-quality cells (>15% mitochondrial DNA, nCount_RNA < 1000, and nFeature_RNA < 200) and doublets were removed (51). Filtered datasets were used for all downstream analyses and included P2 samples of 11,834, 7208, 8286, and 11,752 cells for UA, 12, 17, and 28 dpa time points; GSE267446 P3 samples of 11,499, 6918, 3039, 5414, 7947, and 8591 cells for UA, 11, 12, 14, 17, and 28 dpa time points; and for validation, GSE135985 P2 samples of 1165, 917, and 3356 cells for 10, 10, and 14 dpa time points, respectively (6, 7). Each amputation and time point underwent individual normalization, identification of variable features, scaling, cluster identification, and dimensional reduction.

Integration of datasets across amputations and/or time was performed using the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) Integration method in Seurat followed by renormalization, scaling, cluster identification, and dimensional reduction. The broad fibroblast population for each dataset was identified and subsetted by marker genes Pdgfrα and Lumican, followed by rescaling and clustering. DEGs for subpopulations were identified using the Seurat function FindAllMarkers with min.pct = 0.25, adj.pval < 0.05, and avg.log2FC > 1.00. DEGs between time points and between P2 and P3 fibroblasts were identified using the Seurat function FindMarkers with min.pct = 0.25, adj.pval <0.05, and avg.log2FC > 0.58. All GO term and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were performed using ClusterProfiler v4.10.0 (17). Statistical significance for fibroblast subpopulation changes through time or between P2 and P3 contribution was determined using a previously described differential proportion analysis pipeline (21). SeuratExtend (52) was used to calculate z-scores for DEGs and generation of z-score heatmaps.

### Generation of recombinant AAV constructs and stocks

AAV-CAG-GFP pseudotypes (2/6, 2/8, 2/9, 2/7m8, and 2/PHP.S) were obtained from the Boston Children Hospital Viral Core. Recombinant AAV constructs were cloned into the pAAV2-CAG-tdTomato backbone (Addgene, #59462) where tdTomato was excised with Bam HI and Eco RI restriction enzymes. Full-length mouse cDNAs for Ccl2 (NM_011333.3), Ccn3 (NM_010930.5), Cxcl2 (NM_009140.2), Mest (NM_008490.2), Pcolce2 (NM_029620.2), and Prelp (NM_054077.4) were amplified from oligoDT primed mouse e12.5 cDNA libraries. Gene-specific primers with AAV backbone homology tails were used for amplification with Primestar GLX DNA polymerase (Takara Bio) (table S7). Amplicons were used for Gibson assembly using New England Biolabs (NEB) HiFi Assembly Mix, and clones were maintained in NEB Stable E. coli (New England Biolabs). All plasmids were DNA sequence verified by whole plasmid sequencing at Plasmidsaurus. Endotoxin-free plasmid DNA for each construct was prepared and sent to SignaGen Laboratories for AAV6 production. Titers of all AAV stocks were verified by BCH viral core or SignaGen via qPCR viral genome copy number titration with controls for background and DNA contamination. Certified titers were as follows: AAVPHP.S-GFP 4.2E13 vg/ml, AAV7m8-GFP 2.1E13 vg/ml, AAV8-GFP 2.0E13 vg/ml, AAV6-GFP 2.57E13 vg/ml, AAV9-GFP 3.13E13 vg/ml, AAV6-Ccl2 2.73E13 vg/ml, AAV6-Ccn3 4.15E13 vg/ml, and AAV6-Cxcl2 1.69E13 vg/ml.

### Section HCR-FISH, immunohistochemistry, and histology

Collected digits were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at 4°C overnight, followed by decalcification with Decalcifying Solution-Lite (Sigma-Aldrich) or with Surgipath Decalcifier I (Leica Biosystems). Tissues were processed through a 5 to 30% sucrose gradient and then embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) freezing medium (Tissue-Tek) for cryosectioning on a Leica CM3050s cryostat.

For HCR-FISH, 18-μm sections were processed following a previously reported protocol using the Molecular Instruments v3.0 kit (6). Commercial Pi16 and Anxa8 v3.0 probes (NM_023734.3 and NM_013473.4, respectively; Molecular Instruments v3.0) were used with appropriate amplification hairpins for multiplexing and counterstained with DAPI. To reduce background noise, a TrueVIEW autofluoresence quenching kit (Vector Laboratories) was used. Z-stack images were captured on a Zeiss LSM880 confocal microscope and processed in Fiji.

For immunohistochemistry (IHC), 18-μm sections were blocked with 10% goat serum in phosphate buffered saline with Tween-20 (PBST) and incubated with primary antibody at 4°C overnight; anti-GFP (1:1000; Aves Labs, GFP-1020), anti-VIM (1:200, Novus, NB300-233), anti-RUNX2 (1:200; Abcam, ab192256), anti-F4/80 (1:100; Bio-Rad, MCA497GA), anti-SP7 (1:2000; Abcam, ab22552). Tissues were incubated with appropriate Cyanine3 (Cy3)- or Alexa Fluor 647 (A647)-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature followed by PBST washes and DAPI staining. Slides were mounted in Fluoromount (Southern Biotech) and imaged on a Zeiss LSM880 confocal microscope, capturing z-stack images. Max intensity projections were generated and processed in Fiji (53). High cell density precluded reliable association of DAPI+ nuclei with GFP+ cytoplasm; thus, total GFP signal normalized to total DAPI signal was used as a proxy. GFP per DAPI signal values for each relevant image were quantified in Fiji, with DAPI quantified using the threshold, watershed, and analyze particles functions with follow-up manual annotations. Consistency of GFP expression was evaluated in biological replicate, and quantification was obtained from three areas with high GFP expression for each representative image. Percentage of GFP+ cells coexpressing either VIM or RUNX2 was manually counted; three technical replicates were performed.

Fourteen-micrometer sections were made for 28 dpa histological staining. The Masson’s Trichrome Staining Kit (Polysciences) was used for trichrome staining following the manufacturer’s protocol for frozen sections. For Safranin O/Fast Green staining, slides were stained with Safranin O and Fast Green (Sigma-Aldrich) as previously described (54). Bright-field imaging was performed with a Leica DM2000 upright microscope followed by image processing and analysis in Fiji. The area of connective tissue aggregation distal to the P2 bone was calculated in Fiji.

### Quantitative polymerase chain reaction

To validate overexpression of each gene of interest following AAV injection, 18 P2- or P3-injected digits were collected at 12 dpa (6 dpi). Tissues were homogenized and lysed in TRIzol (Invitrogen) using Navy Eppendorf RNA lysis tubes in a Bullet Blender Storm24 machine (Next Advance) at 4°C. Subsequent RNA extraction was performed following standard TRIzol protocol. cDNA was generated using the SuperScript IV First Strand Synthesis kit primed with oligo-dT (Invitrogen). qPCR was performed with gene-specific primers for Ccl2, Ccn3, Cxcl2, Mest, Pcolce2, and Prelp (table S7) including those previously published (36, 46, 55–58) and SsoAdvanced Universal SYBR green mastermix (Bio-Rad) on a QuantStudio 5 Real-time PCR machine. ΔCt was calculated using Gapdh as a housekeeping gene with in-plate technical triplicates. Relative mRNA expression was calculated using the 2(−ΔΔCt) method with normalization to the respective untreated sample. All qPCR experiments were further performed in triplicate.

### Whole mount digit bone analysis

Alizarin red skeletal staining was used to assess P3 bone regeneration, and 18 digits per AAV group were collected at 28 dpa and stained as previously reported (59). All stained P3 bones were imaged in 50% glycerol with a Leica M165FC stereomicroscope. Quantification of P3 2D area and bone length was performed in Fiji. Bone length was measured from the midpoint of the P2/P3 joint to the distal tip of the bone, and the bone area was measured as the total pixels inside the bone perimeter excluding the P2 and sesamoid bones. Relative area/length percent was calculated by normalizing each value to the average control value. Statistical significance was calculated by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by post hoc t tests with Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing.

Differential calcein and alizarin complexone staining was used to assess new bone growth post–P2 amputation. For all AAV groups, intraperitoneal calcein (10 mg/kg; Sigma-Aldrich) was given immediately following P2 amputations, and intraperitoneal alizarin complexone (30 mg/kg; Sigma-Aldrich) was given 2 days prior (26 dpa) to harvest (60). Eighteen digits per AAV group were collected at 28 dpa and dehydrated in 100% ethanol at 96°C for 24 hours. Digits were cleared in 1% KOH for 24 hours and then stored in 50% glycerol. Digits were imaged with a Leica M165FC epifluorescent steromicroscope. Images were processed, and new bone growth was quantified in Fiji. Preexisting bone was masked, and the remaining alizarin-stained bone was quantified to determine new bone growth area and length of the bone from amputation site using the distal calcein front to the distal tip of bone (fig. S6, J to J”’).

All P3 alizarin red and P2 calcein-alizarin complexone 28 dpa digits also underwent microCT scanning. Digits were scanned on a Scanco Medical μCT 35 system at 55 kVp, 145 μA, 8 W with 600-ms integration time, and a voxel size of 7 μm in 25 to 50% glycerol. Each scan was converted to a DICOM file and analyzed using the 3D Slicer image computing platform (61). 3D segmentation models were made for both P2 and P3 scanned bones; volume and surface area were quantified for the P3 bones. Statistical significance of 3D volume and surface area was calculated by one-way ANOVA followed by post hoc t tests with Bonferroni correction. To evaluate D-V and A-P P3 bone widths while controlling for length, the P-D length of each digit was scaled to 0 to 100%. The mean and SD for D-V and A-P bone widths was calculated at every 2% of P-D length. Statistically significant regions for indication in Fig. 4L were determined by a minimum of two consecutive intervals each with P < 0.05.

### Statistical analysis

Statistical significance in differential gene expression for single-cell data was assessed using the Seurat package FindAllMarkers and FindMarkers functions. Significance in populations was determined with an established differential proportion analysis pipeline (21). Data in bar graphs are shown as mean ± SD, while box plots are median ± interquartile range. All statistical analysis was performed in R v4.3.1. A two-tailed Student’s t test was used to determine significance between two groups. One-way ANOVA with post hoc t test with Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg correction was used for multigroup analyses. MANOVA was used when assessing D-V and A-P bone widths along the bone length. Statistically significant values were determined as P or adjusted P < 0.05.
